name: Urðarbrunnr
material: Sacred spring beneath a root of Yggdrasil
powers: The well of fate from which the Norns shape the destinies of all beings.
description: Urðarbrunnr, the well of fate that lies beneath the root of the world tree Yggdrasil, beside which the three Norns dwell and shape the fates of men. The gods hold their council there, and swans swim in the well. Each day the Norns water the tree with its clay-white water and dew so that it never withers, making the well the source of all destiny in Norse myth.

name: Witch Broom
material: Birch twigs bound to a handle
powers: Carries the rider to the witches' sabbath mountain Blåkulla.
description: The broom (kvast) that, in Swedish folk belief, carried witches to Blåkulla, the witches' sabbath mountain, especially on Maundy Thursday before Easter. The 'påskkärring', the Easter witch, was thought to ride a broom, or a cow, goat, or pitchfork, to Blåkulla. People blocked chimneys and hid brooms behind stoves to stop the flights, and the belief shaped Sweden's Easter-witch custom.
source: Swedish belief in the Easter witches of Blåkulla

name: The Black Book (Sortebog)
powers: Used by cunning folk to heal the sick, find stolen goods, and undo witchcraft.
description: A handwritten book of prayers, charms, and remedies kept by Danish cunning folk, the 'black book' or Cyprianus, named after the apocryphal magician-bishop Cyprianus of Antioch. The books mixed church prayers with healing formulas against disease, worms, and bewitchment. Hundreds survive in Danish archives as evidence of a living folk magic that continued well into the 19th century.

name: The War Shield of Neith
powers: Emblem of the goddess of war and of weaving.
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver. The symbol is attested as her sign from early Egyptian writing, painted on her temple walls and on votive objects, and the classical authors Plutarch and Herodotus described it. It is one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt.
source: Neith emblem on early votives; Plutarch, De Iside

name: The Wesekh Collar
powers: Bestowed solar protection and divine favor on its wearer.
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest by pharaohs, queens, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads capped by golden falcon-headed terminals. Such collars were given as royal gifts and buried with the dead, who are shown receiving them from deities; Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, and stone. The wesekh lent its wearer solar protection and divine favor.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone head that shrieked in flight, used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges and ambushes across the steppe. Described by Persian and Chinese chroniclers, the whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns

name: Wampum Belt
material: Quahog and whelk shell beads woven into belts
era: Eastern Woodlands tradition to the present
powers: Records treaties and laws in a living web of shell.
description: Belts woven from purple and white shell beads that served Eastern Woodlands peoples, especially the Haudenosaunee, as records of treaties, laws and historic events; the patterns carried the meaning read aloud at councils. The Great Law of Peace and the Hiawatha belt are among the most celebrated. Colonists adopted wampum as trade currency, a role that reshaped but never erased its ceremonial use.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and colonial records

name: War Bonnet
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and others)
material: Eagle feathers on a hide cap or band
powers: Each feather marks an honor earned in war or ceremony.
description: The grand headdress of upright eagle feathers worn by Plains chiefs, each feather earned by bravery or a vision and the whole assembled with ceremony. The straight-up bonnet familiar from photographs became prominent in the nineteenth century; earlier forms differed widely. Feathers could also be earned for deeds in peace, and the bonnet is worn with respect as a symbol of leadership.
source: Plains oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Witch Bottle
material: Stoneware or glass bottle with pins, nails, hair and urine
powers: Traps the witch's harm and turns it back on her.
description: A bottle packed with pins, nails, hair and sometimes urine, sealed and hidden in a wall, chimney or hearth to draw a witch's spell into itself and break it, a practice brought from Europe to colonial America. Scores of bottles have been found bricked into old American and English buildings. The charm offers the bottle as a decoy and a trap, its sharp contents meant to wound the witch in return.
source: Colonial American folk magic and archaeological finds

name: Woomera
description: Wooden spear-throwing lever of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, a handle with a peg or socket that lengthens the arm to hurl a spear with greater force and distance. Made from a flat or curved branch shaped with stone tools and fixed with resin, the woomera is a hunting and fighting weapon and a sacred object in initiation, when it may bear the engraved designs of the clan.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of central and western Australia
source: Ethnographic records of Aboriginal hunting technology

name: Waka Taua (Māori War Canoe)
description: Māori war canoe, a long carved vessel of up to forty paddlers that carried war parties on raids and conveyed chiefs in ceremony. Built from a single totara trunk with carved prow and stern posts, the waka taua was a symbol of tribal mana, and its launching and naming were accompanied by ritual and karakia.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Māori naval technology

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is Polish folk paper-cutting, most famously the colourful layered cutouts of Łowicz, made with sheep shears from dyed paper. Designs show birds, suns, flowers and village scenes, and were pasted on walls and beams to brighten rural homes, particularly in Mazovia and Kurpie regions.
